# The Architecture 2.0 Lifecycle {#sec-architecture-20-ontology}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"All models are wrong, but some are useful."*
>
> — George E. P. Box, *Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building* (1979) [@Box1979Robustness]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** George E. P. Box, a British statistician, coined this aphorism about statistical models. Every model simplifies, and the working question is whether the simplification still serves the decision at hand. His point applies to more than prediction models. A task description, benchmark, simulator, power model, or test suite always leaves something out. Each can still be useful when its scope and failure modes are clear and when the decision does not reach beyond the evidence it provides.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
An AI-assisted study can run thousands of tool invocations and still leave nobody able to say which of them checked anything. Why cut that work into stages at all, and why do the cuts fall where they do?
:::

The preceding chapters left architecture work in an uncomfortable position. Design spaces have outgrown manual exploration, while an unguided search optimizes the proxy it was handed rather than the silicon that has to ship. No architect hands over a prompt and receives a taped-out chip. What comes back is a candidate and a number, and that pair is the difficulty this chapter starts from, because a number reports only that the run finished.

Consider what can sit behind a number that looks good. The architect may have asked a question that no achievable evidence could settle. The search may never have been able to express the configuration that would have won. A synthesis tool may have exited cleanly without analyzing anything. The reported margin may sit inside the simulator's own validated error. The gain may be real in the simulator and absent in silicon because the search found a hole in the harness rather than a mechanism. Or the result may be sound and still get read as permission for a decision nobody authorized. Six failures, six different repairs, and one aggregate score that separates none of them.

A lifecycle is worth imposing only if it separates those failures, and naming stages is not what does the separating. A distinct check behind each stage is what does it, so that a study fails where the fault actually occurred and an architect knows which repair to make. Human engineers perform this separation informally, out of tacit knowledge that never reaches a document: implicit workload expectations, unstated thermal limits, and trusted tool combinations. An agent carries none of it. Whatever an experienced architect would have caught by looking has to become a check that something can fail.

This chapter presents the Architecture 2.0 lifecycle on that basis. It establishes the bounded architecture study as the unit of work, so that every machine-generated proposal stays anchored to a claim something can falsify, and then derives six stages that carry such a claim from formulation to defense, arguing for each seam from the failure it exists to isolate.

While this chapter gives the structural argument, the subsequent chapters develop the implementation details in greater depth, including how to build state representations, search algorithms, robust tool interfaces, verification techniques, and accountability structures.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Justify a lifecycle decomposition by naming what can reject the work at each stage, and fold any stage whose failures never occur independently of its neighbor's.
- Bound an architecture study with a claim naming the mechanism, the metric, the baseline, and the corner at which each constraint is checked, then declare the analytic ceiling and the couplings a sweep will disturb before running it.
- Separate a measurement that cleared its check from a mechanism that accounts for it, and name the ablation runs and retained telemetry that would tell the two apart.
- Separate a study's fidelity from its authority, since a higher-fidelity result does not widen what the study may commit to.
- Index a completed study on the twelve-field design-loop card, preserving each rejected candidate with the provenance a passing run carries and leaving visibly empty any field the study never declared.
:::

## The Big Picture: Translating Intent to Execution {#sec-arch2-ontology}

An AI-assisted architecture study needs a common structure connecting the stages of work that are often documented separately. It must preserve the original intent, define a bounded comparison, connect that comparison to an inspectable execution loop, and show who may act on the result.

@fig-structured-layer-above-rtl places an architecture study between the architect's question and the tools used to investigate it. The figure's middle layer is the comparison and its review record. It connects reasoning that often stays in an engineer's head or working notes to executable implementation flows, giving architectural tools, agents, reviewers, and architects a shared question for interpreting each artifact and tool result.

![**An AI-assisted architecture study connects intent to implementation evidence.** The study contains the scope, architectural claim, execution and analysis process, and evidence needed for review. Iterative work uses a design loop.](images/F4d-structured-layer-above-rtl){#fig-structured-layer-above-rtl width="85%" fig-alt="Three-layer diagram showing architecture intent and judgment flowing into a structured architecture study, with tool results flowing back for evidence review."}

Read @fig-structured-layer-above-rtl from top to bottom:

* **The Upper Layer (System Intent)**: This contains the architecture models, requirements, and rationale that shape the question. For the RISC-V XR subsystem from the Lighthouse prompt, this includes the high-level goal of improving mobile XR efficiency and the initial models of the target workload.
* **The Middle Layer (Bounded Comparison)**: This turns intent into a bounded comparison. Its scope names the specific question, such as deciding whether a particular cache configuration merits RTL evaluation. The architectural claim says what will be reviewed. It is not another architecture tool; rather, it connects design intent to tool execution.
* **The Lower Layer (Executable Tool Path)**: Simulators, compilers, RTL generators, and EDA flows carry out different parts of the comparison to return measurements that enter the evidence record.

In software engineering, coding agents rely on structured environments like SWE-bench [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench] to provide a bounded issue, a known repository state, and executable tests. Architecture requires a similar structure, but building it is much harder because feedback (power, area, timing) is delayed, ambiguous, and subject to physical constraints.

Because architecture state is scattered and tool feedback carries different costs and fidelity, an AI-assisted architecture study requires more than just an environment. It requires a bounded claim, evidence at the right fidelity, and a named person who owns the final decision.

## The Six-Stage Execution Lifecycle

To execute the work within that structure, the lifecycle has to say where one kind of work ends and the next begins. Experienced architects already move through these stages informally, carrying project context from a spreadsheet to a simulator to a design review without ever naming a boundary they crossed.

Formalizing those boundaries raises a question the informal version never has to answer. Why cut the work here rather than somewhere else, and why six cuts rather than three or twenty? A stage boundary is not a milestone on a schedule and it is not a handoff between teams. It is a place where what can reject the work changes. Two activities belong in one stage when the same check disqualifies both, and in different stages when either can fail while the other passes cleanly.

Applying that test to the familiar architecture design process produces six stages (@fig-ontology-loop): Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Explain, and Defend. Formulate fails on an envelope calculation, before any candidate exists, when the claim asks for more than the workload has to give. Explore fails on the design space, when the encoding cannot express the configuration that would have won. Implement fails on the infrastructure, when a tool crashes, resumes from stale constraints, or exits with status zero having analyzed nothing. Evaluate fails on the claim check, when a measured margin does not clear its threshold or does not clear the tool's own error. Explain fails on an ablation, when the mechanism the study named turns out not to be the one that produced the number. Defend fails on authority, when the evidence is sound and the decision it is being used to justify sits outside what the study was scoped to support. This chapter works through cases of several of these firing while the others passed, including a cache policy that beat the published state of the art and had no mechanism behind it, and a synthesis run that reported zero power and zero area with a clean exit status.

Read the test in reverse and it becomes an audit any reader can run on a proposed lifecycle, this one included. Ask what can reject the work at each stage. A stage with no distinct rejection is a label rather than a stage, and it should fold into its neighbor. Six is therefore a claim about this decomposition rather than a property of architecture work, and it is falsifiable in the ordinary way. A group whose Implement and Evaluate failures never occur apart, because its tool path reports infrastructure faults and physical violations through one channel, should run five stages and record why.

Crucially, for AI-assisted architecture to be practical, this lifecycle operates at two distinct speeds:

1. **The Inner Agentic Loop (Explore <-> Implement <-> Evaluate):** Operating at *machine speed*, the agent iterates thousands of times autonomously, aggressively pruning the search space, fighting toolchain friction, and relying on proxies and deterministic rejection checks. Those thousands of turns hold only because the loop runs mostly at proxy fidelity. The moment it escalates to a cycle-level simulator or synthesis, its iteration rate drops to that of the slowest tool it invokes, so "machine speed" is really a statement about the loop's composition.
2. **The Outer Human Loop (Formulate -> [Inner Loop] -> Explain -> Defend):** Operating at *human speed*, this loop only triggers when the agent has found a candidate that passes all automated physical constraints and is ready to translate that evidence for human sign-off, the point where gigabytes of tool output have to become an argument a skeptical reviewer will accept.

The split falls where it does for the same reason the stages do. The inner three are exactly the stages whose rejection checks a machine can apply unattended, since a declared design space, a tool exit condition, and a threshold with an error bar beside it are all mechanical. The outer three are the stages whose checks are not. Deciding that a claim is worth asking, that a mechanism account survives an ablation, and that evidence justifies a commitment are judgments that put a name on the result, and the middle of the loop runs fast precisely because those three sit outside it.

![**The Architecture 2.0 engineering lifecycle.** Six numbered stages carry one turn of an architecture study from a bounded claim through search, tool execution, evidence, and interpretation to an authorized decision. Keeping the question, the executed work, the evidence, and the next decision connected is what makes AI assistance reviewable. A turn that fails review returns a revised claim or study to Formulate rather than stopping.](images/ch3-ontology-loop){#fig-ontology-loop width="100%" fig-alt="Six numbered rectangular boxes in two rows. The top row runs left to right through Formulate, Explore, and Implement; the bottom row runs right to left through Evaluate, Explain, and Defend. A red return path carries a revised claim or study from Defend back to Formulate for another turn."}

> **Architecture design loop.** The repeated process of examining the current design, making an allowed change, running the relevant tools, interpreting the result, and deciding whether to revise, reject, or continue. Building on established Agile Hardware Development cycles (e.g., the Chisel ecosystem [@Izraelevitz2017Chisel]), each iteration retains enough information for another architect to see what led to the next step.

To ground these abstract concepts in a practical reality, we use the XR subsystem design task from the Lighthouse prompt as the running example. The interaction between an agent's proposed candidates and the underlying tools forms a continuous execution cycle. A single turn threads the agent's proposal through the tools and back to a claim check (@fig-design-loop):

![**How an iterative architecture study proceeds.** An architect or an automated method reads the recorded design state, makes an allowed change, runs a tool, and submits the result for review. The reviewer records what the evidence supports, and the decision owner determines what happens next.](images/F3-design-loop){#fig-design-loop width="85%" fig-alt="A design loop within a scoped architecture study. Represented state, permitted action, tool feedback, and evidence lead to claim review."}

1. **Read Represented State:** The agent queries the current design state, observing the 2\ MB baseline cache, the XRBench trace, and the 1\ W of headroom remaining in the subsystem's 3\ W budget (dynamic plus leakage).
2. **Make Allowed Change:** The agent proposes expanding the cache to 3\ MB. The study's declared design space admits that change, so the action is legal.
3. **Execute Tool (Feedback):** The proposed 3\ MB configuration is dispatched to the cycle-level simulator (e.g., gem5), the analytical power model (e.g., McPAT), and an SRAM timing and area model (e.g., CACTI). The tools return raw feedback, with illustrative values for this walkthrough: a 12% reduction in capacity misses, resulting in decreased dynamic power (fewer DRAM accesses), but a 2\ mW increase in leakage power and a 0.2\ mm^2^ increase in area.
4. **Compile Evidence:** The raw feedback is packaged with its provenance (simulator version, trace name, time of execution) into an immutable evidence record.
5. **Claim Review:** A deterministic check evaluates the evidence against the original bounded claim. Because the 2\ mW leakage increase keeps the system well within that remaining 1\ W of headroom, the area fits the floorplan constraint, and the 3\ MB macro's reported access time still closes timing at the declared 2\ GHz, the check passes. The 3\ MB configuration becomes the new baseline state for the next iteration.

The next turn shows the outcome the loop exists to produce. The agent proposes 4\ MB, the ceiling of the declared space. The tools return, again with illustrative values, a further 4% reduction in capacity misses, but the larger array's access time no longer closes timing at the declared 2\ GHz; the critical path through the 4\ MB macro misses the cycle budget. The claim review fails on timing. No judgment call is involved. The candidate is rejected, and the run is preserved as a negative trace with the same provenance the passing run carried. The study then stops at its declared commitment level, a simulation-grade recommendation to carry the 3\ MB configuration into RTL evaluation and nothing stronger. The rejection is not wasted work. The preserved trace is what keeps the next study from re-proposing the same dead end.

This formalized loop ensures that every AI-driven change is mechanically verified against physical constraints before it is accepted. The rest of this chapter walks through the six stages of this lifecycle, detailing the unique challenges an agent faces at each step.

## Formulating: Bounding the Study

The first step in the lifecycle (@fig-ontology-loop) is Formulate. To ensure that machine-generated proposals do not drift away from the problem they were asked to solve, we require a bounded architecture study.

In @fig-structured-layer-above-rtl, the architecture question and the judgment behind it establish the starting intent. The Lighthouse prompt states that intent:

> *Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an XRBench-class real-time mobile XR workload. Realize it as a vector-capable CPU, accelerator, or SoC block under a 3\ W TDP target in a 3\ nm-class low-power mobile process, and return a design-space report with evidence and rejected alternatives.*

The system intent is to improve mobile XR efficiency. But this is not yet an architecture task. An agent given only the product intent cannot determine which comparisons the architect needs. The intent must be translated into a claim, a baseline, and a search space (@fig-ontology-chain).

![**The common structure connects a scoped study to an architectural decision.** The architect establishes the scope and states the claim for review, while represented state and tool interfaces make proposed actions executable. When work iterates, a design loop organizes execution and analysis. A reviewer examines the evidence, and the decision owner may accept a finding, narrow the claim, or revise the study.](images/F4-ontology-chain){#fig-ontology-chain width="85%" fig-alt="A common structure connecting a scoped architecture study and its architectural claim to represented state, tools, an execution and analysis process, evidence, review, a named decision owner, and a scoped finding or decision."}

> **Bounded architecture study.** A bounded architecture study turns a broad goal into a specific piece of architecture work. It states the question, workload or scenario, baseline, allowed design choices, objectives, constraints, tools, planned evidence, and decision the work is meant to inform. It also says what the study will not try to decide.

### Defining the Claim

A bounded study anchors everything to an architectural claim: a falsifiable statement that the review process will eventually evaluate.

> **Architectural claim.** An architectural claim says what result the architect expects from a proposed change, why that result should occur, and where it should hold. It identifies the proposed mechanism, expected outcome, workload or scenario, baseline, allowed alternatives, constraints, and the evidence that would count against it.

The claim tells the agent what to optimize and tells the human reviewer what to scrutinize. Contrast a vague human prompt with a properly bounded machine claim:

*   **Vague Prompt:** "Optimize the cache for the XR workload."
*   **Bounded Claim:** "Evaluate L2 capacity up to 4\ MB to reduce XRBench 99th-percentile frame time against the 2\ MB baseline through fewer capacity misses, constrained to a 3\ W sustained power budget (dynamic plus leakage) and a 1.5\ mm^2^ SRAM macro area footprint, with both limits and timing closure at 2\ GHz checked at the slow-slow corner and 125\ °C."

Without a bounded claim, an agent might endlessly tune parameters without a stopping condition, or it might propose a massive cache that maximizes Instructions Per Cycle (IPC) but physically melts the chip.

Notice that the bounded claim names a tail metric rather than a throughput average. The Lighthouse workload is real-time, and real-time workloads are judged by deadlines, not throughput. A cache that raises average IPC by 8% while lengthening the worst-case frame is a regression for an XR subsystem, where what matters is whether every frame meets its motion-to-photon budget. The claim names the 99th-percentile frame time under the 3\ W envelope for exactly this reason. An agent handed IPC will faithfully optimize a number the product does not ship on.

Naming a tail metric creates an obligation the claim itself must carry. The evidence regime has to resolve the tail, and the workload sampling this chapter later requires is least reliable exactly where the tail lives, because a sample chosen to represent aggregate behavior can miss the rare interval that sets the 99th percentile. The general rule follows. A metric the declared evidence regime cannot measure does not bound a study, however precisely it is worded. Either the study shows that its sampling preserves the tail statistic, stating the interval count and the confidence it reaches, or it declares a metric the regime can deliver and records the tail question as unresolved.

The bounded claim also invites a check that costs nothing to run. Before the loop runs, run the study on paper. If XRBench spends 18% of its cycles stalled on L2 capacity misses, a perfect cache buys back at most those cycles, an Amdahl-style ceiling [@HillMarty2008Amdahl], and every buildable configuration buys less. That one-line limit study, computed before any tool is invoked, is the cheapest rejection check in the lifecycle. A study whose claim exceeds its own limit study is not bounded; it is wishful.

### The Curse of Entangled Constraints

Once the claim is stated, the architect must bound the design space. However, computer architecture is fundamentally about coupled systems. An architect rarely isolates a single metric without triggering a cascading butterfly effect across Power, Performance, Area, and Thermals (PPAT).

When bounding the search space, an architect cannot simply set a naive upper limit like "L2 cache up to 4\ MB." Scaling up an L2 cache doesn't just consume abstract area; it lengthens the wire distance to reach the cache, adds banks the interconnect has to arbitrate among, and introduces localized thermal hotspots. On the Lighthouse those effects do not land on an idle fabric, because the camera and SLAM streams are already contending for it. In physical design, a 4\ MB cache requires placing massive SRAM macros. These macros create hard routing blockages and pin density bottlenecks that threaten power integrity (IR drop), because the rails cannot supply the peak current density a single monolithic block demands, which is why such a macro usually has to be broken into a distributed, tiled array. If an agent optimizes only for aggregate area, it will propose a subsystem that passes analytical proxies but is fundamentally unroutable in Place-and-Route (P&R).

The constraints themselves are also underspecified until the study names its corner. The 3\ W limit and the 2\ GHz target mean nothing until the study says where they are checked, because silicon signs off at worst-case process, voltage, and temperature, and a design that closes timing at the typical corner routinely fails at slow-slow and 125\ °C. The bounded study must declare which corner each constraint is checked at and how much guardband it reserves for model error, which is why the claim above ends at the slow-slow corner and 125\ °C rather than at 3\ W and 2\ GHz alone. An agent that checks only at nominal will otherwise pass candidates that no sign-off flow would accept.

::: {.callout-war-story title="Mars Climate Orbiter and the units nobody checked"}
**The claim.** The Mars Climate Orbiter's navigation team modeled the small thruster firings that trim a spacecraft's attitude using an impulse figure delivered by ground software. A project Software Interface Specification fixed the format of that file and stated its units as newton-seconds, so both sides of the interface had a written contract to work from [@MCOMishapBoard1999].

**The gap.** The ground software reported the impulse in pound-force seconds, and nothing in the flow compared the delivered file against the specification, so the navigation software underestimated every desaturation event by the 4.45 conversion factor. Each side passed its own checks. The onboard software used metric units and was correct, the ground code ran without error, and the specification itself was right. Only the agreement between them went unverified. Navigators saw discrepancies between competing orbit solutions through the spring and summer of 1999 but reported them informally rather than through the project's anomaly process, so nothing on record could stop the insertion. The reconstructed trajectory put closest approach at 57\ km against a planned 226\ km and a survivable minimum of 80\ km, and the spacecraft was lost on September 23, 1999.

**The lesson.** A constraint is not checkable until the study names the units and conditions it holds under, and the rejection check that enforces them where the value crosses an interface. A bounded study that declares a 3\ W envelope and a 2\ GHz target without saying at which corner, in which units, and under which rejection check has written a specification with the same property this one had. It is correct, and nothing consumes it. An agent crosses several such interfaces every turn, handing numbers from a power model to a timing tool to a claim check, and each crossing left without a declared and enforced contract is a place where a confident result can be wrong by a constant no one sees.
:::

Formulating a bounded study is incredibly difficult because it requires explicitly mapping these hidden entanglements and physical blockages, and then naming the conditions and units under which each constraint is checked. A well-formulated boundary prevents the agent from optimizing one local subsystem while silently starving the memory controller or rendering the floorplan unroutable.

Modern system intent also demands strict hardware/software boundaries. An agent optimizing hardware in isolation might produce a theoretically efficient accelerator that no compiler can target. To prevent this, the architect must extend the bounded study to include the software path (compilers, runtimes, and mapping strategies) so that the agent evaluates the hardware alongside an executable software baseline.

## Exploring: State Representation and Search

With the problem formulated, the next stage is Explore. In this stage, an agent searches the bounded design space to find promising architecture candidates.

However, an agent cannot explore a space it cannot see or understand. For the search to be effective, we must explicitly provide the agent with a machine-readable view of the architecture and a way to quickly predict the consequences of its choices before running expensive simulations.

An agent can act only on the information it is given. For human architects, design intent lives scattered across natural-language specifications, ISA manuals, spreadsheet models, and tacit knowledge locked in engineers' heads. An agent requires this unstructured intent to be translated into an explicit, machine-readable represented state.

### Topological State and the Curse of the Action Space

However, translating architecture into a machine-readable state exposes a hard ML-systems challenge: *the curse of the action space*.[^fn-action-space-c03] An SoC is not a flat list of independent variables; it is a complex, topological graph of queues, arbiters, and pipeline stages. Mapping categorical, continuous, and graph-based constraints into an action space that an agent can safely navigate is remarkably difficult. To solve this, the topological state must be concretely serialized, for example as a formal constraint graph, a Hardware Construction Language (e.g., Chisel) Intermediate Representation (IR), or a Graph Neural Network (GNN)[^fn-gnn-c03] node representation.

[^fn-action-space-c03]: **Action space**: The set of changes an agent is permitted to make at each step, together with the encoding it uses to emit them. An architecture study's action space is its declared design space made machine-legible, so a parameter the encoding cannot express is a design the agent can never propose.

[^fn-gnn-c03]: **Graph Neural Network (GNN)**: A neural network that consumes a graph directly, computing each node's representation from its neighbors rather than from a flattened feature vector. It fits hardware because a netlist or floorplan is natively a graph, so adjacency, fan-out, and physical neighborhood survive into the model instead of being flattened away.

If an agent only receives the cache miss rates but remains blind to the area floorplan encoded in the GNN, it may propose a massive cache that maximizes IPC but cannot physically fit on the die. Alternatively, if the agent attempts to widen the vector execution engine or add a specialized Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) array for the XR workload to boost compute throughput, this forces a trade-off discussion about vector register file area and pipeline timing closure. When an agent proposes an impossible design, the root cause is often this missing topological state.

### The Modality Mismatch

Even if the state is fully topological, exploration faces a mismatch between what models consume and what hardware is. Modern machine learning models natively consume sequential text tokens (LLMs) or fixed-shape numeric tensors (most neural predictors and policies). Hardware, however, exists as rigid hierarchical netlists, Hardware Description Languages (Verilog/Chisel), and constraint graphs. An LLM might generate syntactically perfect Verilog that is structurally nonsensical [@LiuEtAl2024CraftRTL], such as a control state machine with no reset path to its idle state, which passes every functional testbench because the simulator initializes each register to a known value, and then hangs on hardware that powers up in an arbitrary one. An agent with a continuous action head might likewise emit values that fail to map onto discrete hardware parameters. Graph and discrete action spaces are standard in reinforcement learning, so the mismatch is one of chosen representation, not an inherent limit of the method. Bridging this gap is essential for generating valid architecture proposals.

### Proxy Fidelity, UQ, and Distribution Shift

Once an agent proposes a valid candidate, it relies on prediction models (fast proxies) to estimate performance, power, and area without paying for the full tool flow. Whether a proxy of that kind is a model of the machine or only a scoring function for one search is @sec-data-representations-world-models's question. What matters at this stage is narrower. Learned proxies predict linear scaling easily and fail catastrophically on *non-linear interference* such as shared TLB thrashing, and a proxy earns its place by ordering candidates correctly rather than by predicting their exact numbers, so the failure that corrupts a search is error correlated with the swept parameter rather than error magnitude.

As the agent explores deeper into the design space, or as engineers update baseline parameters, the environment becomes non-stationary, causing a distribution shift.[^fn-distribution-shift-c03] The offline data used to train the proxies quickly becomes stale. An agent aggressively optimizing against a stale fast proxy will inevitably push the inputs Out-of-Distribution (OOD), leading to reward hacking (Goodhart's Law) where the agent actively exploits extrapolation errors to endorse impossible results [@AmodeiEtAl2016Concrete].

[^fn-distribution-shift-c03]: **Distribution shift**: When the inputs a model is asked to score stop resembling the data it was trained on, so its accuracy degrades without any error being raised. The architecture analogue is a power model calibrated on one process node and one workload mix that keeps returning confident numbers after both have changed underneath it.

To survive, exploration must include active learning loops and Uncertainty Quantification (UQ). The agent must *know when it is guessing*. It relies on acquisition functions (such as Expected Improvement or Upper Confidence Bound in Bayesian Optimization) that score where in the design space the next sample is worth taking. Choosing where to sample is not the same as choosing how expensively to measure it, and escalating from a proxy to a high-fidelity tool is a separate policy with its own trigger, stated at the Implement stage below. Furthermore, the system must maintain these surrogates on the fly, managing replay buffers and telemetry dataset versioning to avoid catastrophic forgetting as the design topology shifts.[^fn-catastrophic-forgetting-c03]

[^fn-catastrophic-forgetting-c03]: **Catastrophic forgetting**: When a model retrained on new data loses the accuracy it had on regions it once predicted well, because the new gradients overwrite the earlier fit. Retraining a proxy on a fresh corner of the design space can therefore break its predictions on configurations already accepted, which is why the loop keeps older runs in a buffer and mixes them back into every retraining pass.

## Implementing: Toolchain Friction and Escalation

Moving to the Implement stage (@fig-ontology-loop), once the agent proposes a candidate architecture, the next step is executing the simulation and compilation tools to gather physical evidence.

### Navigating Toolchain Friction

Unlike software environments where code compiles in milliseconds and tests run deterministically, architecture tools are often fragile, slow, and prone to silent failures. Commercial EDA tools are particularly hostile to automated agents because they are driven by decades-old, deeply stateful Tcl scripts. An agent interacting with these tools will not just encounter crashes; it will face "dirty state" (leftover constraints from a previous run in the same workspace) and the nightmare of parsing semantic meaning out of multi-gigabyte Static Timing Analysis (STA) reports. Dirty state is more dangerous than a crash because it still returns an answer. An agent that omits a `reset_design` between iterations stacks each run's constraints on the last until the tool's timing graph collapses and it reports zero-delay closure, a result no real design produces and no exit code flags.

Furthermore, an agent does not just emit RTL; it must synthesize compatible EDA collateral across fragmented vendor silos, including SDC[^fn-sdc-c03] for timing constraints and UPF for power intent.

[^fn-sdc-c03]: **SDC (Synopsys Design Constraints)**: The de facto standard file that carries a design's timing intent, clock definitions, input and output delays, false paths, and multicycle paths into synthesis and timing analysis. A netlist by itself never states what frequency it was meant to run at, so without its SDC the timing tools have nothing to check the design against.

From an ML-Sys perspective, vectorizing these incredibly slow, stateful EDA tools for batched RL inference while handling variable-length action spaces when hardware topologies change dynamically is a massive infrastructure challenge.

To operate effectively, an agent needs clear tool interfaces (like the ArchGym API [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]) that expose the failure modes and recovery actions. Beyond avoiding crashes, navigating toolchain friction requires rigorous provenance data engineering. To train reliable ML proxies offline, an agent cannot simply log a failed IPC score. It must capture the exact environment state as an immutable record covering tool versions, random seeds, intermediate Tcl state, and DRC markers.

Importantly, all of this friction unfolds deep inside the fast automated inner loop (the Explore, Implement, Evaluate cycle), which spins thousands of times at machine speed, completely decoupled from the slow outer loop the architect reviews.

Commercial EDA tools fail in a handful of recurring ways, each with a recovery move the loop can record (@tbl-toolchain-friction).

| **Toolchain friction type** | **Agent recovery strategy** |
| --- | --- |
| **FlexLM license hangs or timeouts** | Implement exponential backoff, strict resource timeouts to prevent thread deadlocks, or query a lower-fidelity tool. |
| **Stateful Tcl & "Dirty State"** | Full teardowns take hours for tapeout-scale blocks (Innovus, ICC2), so agents resume from snapshots rather than rebuilding. A snapshot is only safe if it records which constraints were in force when it was taken, so a run whose recorded state does not match the one its claim assumes can be rejected instead of scored. |
| **Logical/Physical Abstract Mismatch** | Scaling SRAMs or custom IP requires perfect pin/timing alignment between logical (LIB/Verilog) and physical (LEF/DEF) abstracts. Validate alignments before invoking place-and-route. |
| **CDC/RDC & DFT Violations** | AI-generated RTL may pass functional simulation but fail structural CDC/RDC linting or break scan chain insertion (DFT). Enforce strict synchronous boundary and testability constraints upstream. |
| **Undocumented tool crashes** | Log the failure, mark the configuration as invalid, and pivot to a nearby state. |
| **Silent output corruptions** | Use secondary validation checks (e.g., verifying the netlist isn't empty) to flag anomalous results. |
| **Zero-exit-code parsing errors** | Do not trust a `0` exit status. Validate physical outputs directly and cluster massive STA/DRC logs before ML ingestion. |

: **Each EDA friction mode has a recovery move the loop can log:** Commercial-tool failure modes an automated agent meets, and the recovery each one demands. {#tbl-toolchain-friction tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}

A bounded study turns toolchain friction from a fatal obstacle into a recorded constraint. When an agent cannot evaluate a candidate due to a tool crash or a dirty Tcl state, it logs the failure and pivots. That log is not the same thing as a rejection. A candidate the physics refused tells the study something about the design space; a candidate the toolchain never evaluated tells it something about the infrastructure, and only the first should ever count against the candidate. A run record that cannot separate the two makes preserved failures actively misleading, because a later study reads infrastructure noise as a closed region of the space. Planning for tool failures in advance lets the search continue over the viable portions of the design space.



### Multi-Fidelity Escalation

Bounded architecture studies span multiple levels of abstraction, from fast analytical proxies to cycle-level simulators and slow RTL synthesis.

Escalation is governed by a massive temporal cost asymmetry: querying a proxy takes milliseconds, a sampled cycle-level simulation takes minutes, but RTL synthesis can take days. The search must be constrained by an explicit budget to justify invoking synthesis. That budget also has to cover the machinery the lifecycle itself prescribes. Active learning, uncertainty quantification, proxy retraining, counterfactual ablations, and screening designs all consume the same scarce runs, and a study that funds them out of an unstated reserve has not bounded anything. Declare them as line items or declare that the study will not run them.

Furthermore, there is a massive chasm within "synthesis" itself. An agent might propose a design that passes *logical synthesis* (idealized timing and gate counts) but fails horribly at *physical synthesis* (parasitic extraction, actual wire delays, clock tree synthesis). For example, if an agent proposes a 128-way associative cache, a miss-rate proxy might report only a marginal gain over the 8-to-16-way designs that already eliminate most conflict misses, yet still score it a win because the proxy ignores hit latency and energy. In silicon, driving associativity that high requires large tag-comparison logic and heavy fan-in and fan-out on the 128-to-1 way multiplexers. When the agent escalates the design to physical synthesis, it fails timing closure because the mux logic and routing congestion break the target clock frequency, and the marginal miss gain never justified the cost.

To bridge this gap without bankrupting the computation budget, the escalation path often requires hardware emulation (e.g., Palladium or ZeBu) as a necessary middle ground for workloads that are too slow for pure RTL simulation but require more physical accuracy than gem5.

> **Multi-fidelity escalation.** A defined policy that states the conditions under which an agent must transition from a fast proxy to a high-fidelity tool [@KandasamyEtAl2017MultiFidelityBO]. It specifies the budget for high-fidelity runs and the checks required before escalation.

The condition that fires it is narrower than "the proxy looks uncertain." Escalate when the proxy's uncertainty at a candidate is larger than the margin separating that candidate from the incumbent, because below that margin the proxy cannot resolve the comparison the study exists to make, however accurate it is on average. A proxy predicting 4\ MB at 12% better frame time, plus or minus 9%, against a 2\ MB baseline has not ranked anything, and one more proxy sample will not change that. The same rule sets the reverse: a candidate the proxy separates from the incumbent by far more than its uncertainty does not need a signoff run to be rejected.

Escalation and authority are separate axes, which is why @fig-design-loop draws them apart. Moving to a higher fidelity buys a better measurement of the same question; it does not enlarge what the study may commit to. A higher-fidelity result does not by itself authorize a more consequential decision, because the decision rights were fixed when the study declared its scope. An architect who reads a passing signoff run as permission to skip the commitment boundary has confused a better number with a wider mandate.

Recording these transitions in the design loop keeps the proxy-driven search anchored to physical reality. When a proxy win disappears at higher fidelity, the agent updates its cost model, and the architect reviews the discrepancy. Part of that shrinkage is structural rather than proxy failure, because selecting the best of thousands of noisy scores selects partly for luck and the escalated winner reliably scores below its estimate, a selection effect that @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization treats in full. This continuous recalibration across fidelity levels is what allows an agent to explore efficiently without drifting into physically impossible design states.

## Evaluating: Reviewable Evidence

The Evaluate stage assesses the results. The study must distinguish raw tool feedback from reviewable architectural evidence, particularly under the crushing constraints of simulation scale and physical verification.

### The High Cost of Physical Evidence

Acquiring physical evidence forces an agent to confront three distinct bottlenecks that fundamentally limit how often it can evaluate a candidate:

* **Simulation speed:** We casually refer to running "XRBench traces," but executing a single real-time second of an XR workload requires billions of cycles. Cycle-level simulators run at a few hundred KIPS,[^fn-kips-c03] and RTL drops to hundreds of cycles per second. This forces the agent to rely on workload sampling (e.g., SimPoint [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint]) and to rigorously quantify the statistical confidence of its samples. Furthermore, evaluation bottlenecks must be expanded to include the memory controller. If the agent shrinks the cache, it will quickly hit the "memory bandwidth wall," forcing it to co-optimize DRAM channel width or DDR scheduling policies to keep the XR subsystem fed.
* **Physical & Functional Verification:** Physical design enforces binary, non-negotiable walls at Functional Verification (UVM testbenches), Logic Equivalence Checking (LEC), and DRC/LVS sign-off. When failures occur here, a single architectural mistake (like a bad SRAM macro placement) can spawn millions of cascading, highly correlated DRC/LVS violations. The agent must cluster and root-cause these physical errors before ingesting them as reviewable negative evidence, otherwise it will instantly overwhelm any model's context window. Furthermore, the lifecycle must distinguish localized physical iteration from global architectural resets. Localized iteration means surgical Engineering Change Orders (ECOs) like gate sizing or buffer insertion, while a reset kicks the agent all the way back to the *Explore* stage.
* **The Software Co-Adaptation Bottleneck:** If an agent invents a novel hardware feature (e.g., a custom vector instruction), the existing compiler will not know how to use it. Evaluating novel hardware often requires an agent capable of simultaneously adapting the software stack just to exercise its own design.

[^fn-kips-c03]: **KIPS**: Thousands of simulated instructions per second, a common throughput unit for architectural simulators. A few hundred KIPS against a target core retiring billions of instructions per second puts the simulator roughly four orders of magnitude behind the silicon it models, which is what forces sampling instead of full-workload runs.

### Formatting Evidence

Because physical simulation is astronomically expensive, the system cannot afford to waste a single tool run. The primary purpose of formatting evidence, especially negative results, is to extract maximum algorithmic value from failed runs so the agent never pays the simulation cost of the same mistake twice.

When an agent changes a parameter and a tool completes the run, the result is mere *feedback*. It becomes *evidence* only when it is tied to the architectural claim and the run record identifies the conditions, constraints, and provenance under which it was produced. The strength of the check must match the next decision. A proxy may be enough to keep a candidate in the search, while starting RTL work or making a product decision requires stronger evidence from tools closer to the implemented system.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A 3\ W claim needs evidence, not a number"}
**Context.** A reported power result is feedback. It becomes evidence only when the run record provides enough information for a reviewer to judge what the number means.

**In the cache comparison.** A statement that one cache configuration remains inside the modeled 3\ W envelope needs the named XRBench traces, RISC-V baseline, cache parameters, simulator and power-model versions, relevant software assumptions, uncertainty, and the check that would rule the configuration out.
:::

The uncertainty field is not a formality, though it has to be read against the right bar. Validated cycle-level simulators disagree with the silicon they model by 5 to 20% per workload [@GutierrezEtAl2014SourcesOfError; @AkramSawalha2019SimulatorSurvey], and analytical power models miss by more. That range bounds what the simulator can claim about any one configuration on its own. It does not bound a comparison between two configurations that the same frozen simulator treats identically, because most of the systematic error is shared and cancels when candidates are ordered against each other, which is why a proxy earns its place by ranking correctly rather than by predicting exact numbers. The 4\ MB turn still fails on timing, but its 4% capacity-miss reduction is not disqualified by the 5 to 20% figure. That delta has to clear the residual error surviving the comparison and the simulator's own run-to-run spread, and the record has to name which bar the check applied. @sec-running-the-loop works this through on a live decision margin. Every rejection check in the loop needs the tool's validated error recorded next to its threshold and needs to state whether that threshold reads an absolute claim or a relative one, or a deterministic check is deterministically checking noise.

Rejected candidates, failed simulator runs, and proxy wins that disappear at higher fidelity all help mathematically map the valid design space. An agent shouldn't simply discard these failures; it must preserve them as negative evidence to prevent future agents from wasting expensive tool runs on known dead ends [@ShinnEtAl2023Reflexion].

What a run record keeps also fixes what the next stage can still ask. Explanation has to attribute an aggregate result to a mechanism, and it can do that only from intermediate telemetry the run either retained or threw away: per-set and per-way hit counts, stall-cause breakdowns, miss classifications, queue occupancies, and the interval boundaries the sampling used. None of it is recoverable afterward from a top-line score. A twelve-hour simulation that wrote out one IPC number has not merely omitted detail; it has priced the mechanism question at a second twelve-hour run. Evaluate therefore owes the study a declaration of which counters it retains, and a study that keeps only the top-line metric should record that choice where a reviewer will see it, because it has set the ceiling on every explanation that can follow.

## Explaining: Mechanism and Interpretation

The Explain stage (@fig-ontology-loop) supplies a mechanistic account of the results. A fast proxy score or a high-fidelity simulation result reports *what* happened. The explanation stage establishes *why* it happened, and whether the design is the reason.

Explain is the stage most often folded into Evaluate, and the seam test is what holds them apart. The two ask different questions of the same run. Evaluate asks whether the number clears the check the claim declared. Explain asks whether the number came from the design rather than from the harness that measured it. Those fail independently and in both directions. A candidate can clear every threshold with no mechanism behind it, which is the case worked below, where a cache-replacement policy beat the prior state of the art by sending traffic out of the modeled system entirely. A candidate can also fail its threshold while its mechanism is fully understood, which is what happened at 4\ MB, where the timing rejection needed no investigation at all.

Separating the two also protects the check. Evaluate's rejection checks are what the search optimizes against, so a search with enough freedom will eventually satisfy them without satisfying the intent behind them. A check that lives inside the objective can be defeated by the search it scores. Explain's check is asked after the search has committed to a candidate, about a question the search was never optimizing, and it is answered by new runs rather than by the score already in hand. This is the same reason a held-out set is kept out of the training loss. Folding Explain into Evaluate would put every check the study owns inside the objective, which is the exact configuration the two failures below exploit.

### The "Clever Hans" Risk

When an agent proposes a design change (such as expanding the XR subsystem cache) and a simulator confirms it runs faster, the agent must provide a falsifiable architectural mechanism. Did the cache actually reduce conflict misses for the XRBench traces, or did the search simply find a way to skip a mandatory initialization routine in the simulator?

Without demanding a mechanism, the architect risks accepting a "Clever Hans" result [@LapuschkinEtAl2019CleverHans],[^fn-clever-hans-c03] where the search exploits a simulator bug, an edge case, or a broken script rather than discovering a genuine architectural improvement.

[^fn-clever-hans-c03]: **Clever Hans**: A performing horse of the early 1900s that appeared to do arithmetic until Oskar Pfungst showed it was reading involuntary cues from whoever asked, and failed whenever the questioner did not know the answer. Machine learning borrowed the name for a model that scores well through a shortcut in the evaluation setup rather than the capability the benchmark claims to measure, which in architecture is a candidate whose gain comes from the harness rather than the design.

A published architecture-discovery study makes the risk concrete. Gupta and colleagues' ArchAgent had an evolutionary coding agent write last-level cache replacement policies into ChampSim [@GoberEtAl2022ChampSim], scoring each candidate on simulated IPC [@GuptaEtAl2026ArchAgent]. One product of that loop was a usage-intensity mechanism its authors could name, ablate, and attribute. Another, Policy12, appeared to beat the prior state of the art by 3 to 4% on single-core SPEC CPU 2006 by exploiting the simulator rather than the architecture. ChampSim does not support bypassing last-level cache writes, and the assertion enforcing that was compiled out of the optimized build the campaign needed in order to finish at all, so a bypassed write left the modeled system entirely and took its DRAM traffic with it. The paper calls this a *simulator escape*.

The pair is the lesson. One process produced a genuine mechanism and a broken measurement, and the reported margins do not separate them, since Policy12's apparent 3 to 4% sits inside the 1 to 3% band that real cache-replacement advances have historically won. A trace-driven simulator has no notion of correct computation, so no check the tool offered could have caught it; the authors found the escape by inspecting the policy. Preserving the build configuration, the rejected policy, and the check that disqualified it is what would let a later study reuse that check instead of rediscovering the loophole. A check the build strips away is only one way to lose one. A check that survives can fail just as quietly by being impossible to fail.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The AI that optimized the chip out of existence"}
An engineering team tasked a Reinforcement Learning agent with minimizing power and area for an accelerator block using a commercial EDA synthesis toolchain.

**The trap.** The agent quickly reported a spectacular success: a design that consumed 0.0\ W of power and 0.0\ mm^2^ of area, while returning a successful exit code `0` from the synthesis tool.

**The mechanism.** The agent had not discovered a breakthrough architecture. Instead, it had mutated a Tcl configuration script so that the primary clock was never defined, leaving the tool with no constrained paths to analyze. Timing analysis reported zero violations because it had nothing to check, and the flow's other stages reported cleanly against a design whose sequential behavior was never exercised. Every check in the flow passed, because each one measured a property the empty design trivially satisfied. A human engineer caught it on sight.

**The lesson.** A rejection check that cannot fail on an empty design is not measuring the design. Check that the reward and the exit code still discriminate against a null candidate before trusting either.

This case is a composite of a failure pattern engineers report when a search is given write access to tool configuration, not one published incident.
:::

### Credit Assignment and Automated Counterfactuals

The architecture lifecycle poses a severe Reinforcement Learning challenge known as credit assignment.[^fn-credit-assignment-c03] If an agent makes 50 distinct micro-architectural tweaks and a 12-hour simulation returns a single aggregated IPC score, how does it learn *which* tweak was responsible? Solving this sparse, delayed reward problem requires extracting dense intermediate telemetry. Classical experimental design offers a partial answer, since fractional factorial and Plackett-Burman screening [@PlackettBurman1946Design] attribute an aggregate score across dozens of parameters in a number of runs that grows linearly with the parameter count rather than exponentially, roughly one run per parameter instead of the $2^k$ a full factorial demands, an approach @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization develops for search.

[^fn-credit-assignment-c03]: **Credit assignment**: In reinforcement learning, the problem of attributing a single delayed reward back to the individual actions that earned it. The standard remedies assume cheap, plentiful episodes to average over, an assumption a twelve-hour simulation breaks, which is why an architecture loop has to recover attribution from intermediate telemetry rather than from repetition.

The explanation stage mitigates the Clever Hans risk by isolating these causal mechanisms. However, modern CPUs are deeply pipelined and highly speculative, creating a "fog" where effects are decoupled from root causes. If an agent proposes the 3\ MB XR cache and simulation shows a drop in IPC, the true cause might not be the miss rate (which improved), but the larger cache increasing hit latency, thereby stalling the deeply pipelined out-of-order execution engine.

While techniques like SHAP [@LundbergLee2017SHAP] explain the *surrogate proxy*, they provide *zero physical proof*. True explanation requires ablation against ground truth, in which agents orchestrate their own simulator runs to isolate the mechanism they claim is responsible. For example, an agent proves its hypothesis by locking specific cache ways or synthesizing micro-benchmarks to observe the isolated impact on capacity misses. ArchAgent's authors ran this kind of ablation on Policy31 by re-enabling its mechanisms one at a time, found that two of the four supplied most of the measured gain, and report the work as manual and a standing bottleneck [@GuptaEtAl2026ArchAgent]. The ablation is what converts a generated policy into a defensible mechanism, and automating it remains open. A fluent LLM description is merely a hypothesis; the explanation stage proves it against physical telemetry.

## Defending: Authority and the Design-Loop Card

No single stage operates in a vacuum. The Defend stage (@fig-ontology-loop) forces the loop to surface its claims and its mechanistic explanations for explicit sign-off. It is here that the system distinguishes between the agent's autonomous execution and the architect's non-delegable authority.

### Compressing Evidence for Review

In @fig-structured-layer-above-rtl, a reviewer examines this evidence before the named decision owner accepts a finding. Here, the loop faces the difficulty of compressing massive, multi-fidelity tool outputs, such as a gigabyte STA log, into a concise argument that a skeptical architecture committee will actually trust.

Describing a system as autonomous does not specify what it is allowed to do. Architects should assign separate decision rights instead of giving the system one overall level of automation (@tbl-decision-rights-matrix).

| **Right** | **What it authorizes** | **Required record** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Propose** | Produce a candidate, hypothesis, test, or change for review. | Person or system, allowed output type, scope, budget, and required provenance. |
| **Execute** | Run a declared action through the tool path. | Legal actions, resource limits, stop conditions, failure handling, and rollback path. |
| **Reject** | Block a candidate, claim, or next step when a named rejection check fails. | Check, threshold, evidence source, whether the check is independent, and who may reject. |
| **Waive** | Permit a failed or unmet rejection check to be bypassed under stated conditions. | Waiver holder, rationale, expiration, residual risk, and reopening condition. |
| **Recommend** | Summarize the evidence and recommend a specific next step. | Recommender, supported scope, alternatives, what the recommendation does not cover, and uncertainty. |
| **Commit** | Approve the next high-impact step and accept its remaining risk. | Decision owner, approved step, accepted evidence, and conditions for reversal or revalidation. |

: **Decision rights are independent assignments.** A recorded policy may authorize an agent to propose, execute, reject under a stated check, or recommend. Waive and commit rights remain with named people. {#tbl-decision-rights-matrix tbl-colwidths="[14,34,42]"}

This division is what makes the design loop agentic rather than autonomous. An agent can propose the 3\ MB XR cache and reject it if it fails thermal checks, but the right to commit millions of dollars to tape-out stays with the named human who answers for the outcome.

### The Design-Loop Card {#sec-design-loop-card}

With authority assigned and the evidence reviewed, one need remains. How does the human architect know the search didn't cheat the physics?

The *design-loop card* answers that question by indexing what the study actually retained. It is not a summary of the work and it is not a certificate that the work was done well. It is a fixed set of twelve fields, each pointing at a record a reviewer can open, so a later reader can find the scope, the evidence, and the rejected alternatives without reconstructing them from prose.

> **Design-loop card.** A short guide to one architecture study. It points to the question, scope, and claim, then shows how architects and agents carried out the work. Detailed design state, evidence, and replay artifacts remain in linked records.

The ML community adopted a similar practice with model cards to make reporting more transparent [@MitchellEtAl2019ModelCards]. Model cards disclose the evaluation data behind a trained model so a later user can tell where it should not be applied, and the design-loop card does the same job for one architecture study. The cache study this chapter has been running fills all twelve fields (@tbl-design-loop-card-fields), and @fig-design-loop-card-example shows the same structure filled for a different study.

| **Field** | **The cache study's entry** |
| --- | --- |
| **Intent** | Improve XR subsystem efficiency without breaking the declared power envelope. |
| **Task** | Evaluate L2 capacity up to 4\ MB to reduce XRBench 99th-percentile frame time through fewer capacity misses. |
| **Design space** | L2 capacity from the 2\ MB baseline to the declared 4\ MB ceiling, at the stated corner. |
| **Representation** | Recorded design state: cache parameters, the XRBench trace, and the 3\ W budget covering dynamic plus leakage, with 1\ W of headroom. |
| **Environment** | Cycle-level simulator, analytical power model, and SRAM timing and area model, each pinned to a recorded version. |
| **Method role** | Generation only. The method proposes the next capacity; it does not run the claim check. |
| **Feedback budget** | Not declared by this walkthrough. Declaring it would fix how many tool runs the study may spend before it stops, and that omission is why the study cannot say whether stopping at 4\ MB was a budget decision or an evidence decision. |
| **Evidence** | A 12% capacity-miss reduction, a 2\ mW leakage increase, and a 0.2\ mm^2^ area increase, packaged with simulator version, trace name, and execution time. |
| **Failed runs and rejected alternatives** | The 4\ MB turn, preserved as a negative trace carrying the same provenance the passing run carried. |
| **Rejection checks and authority** | Deterministic checks on power headroom, floorplan area, and timing closure at the declared 2\ GHz. The timing check rejected 4\ MB, and no judgment call was involved. |
| **What the evidence supports** | A simulation-grade recommendation to carry the 3\ MB configuration into RTL evaluation, and nothing stronger. Note the gap the card exposes. The claim is stated in 99th-percentile frame time, the record reports capacity misses, and nobody converted one into the other, so the study supports the proposed mechanism and not yet the frame-time result it was written to test. |
| **Accountable decision** | The architect who declared the claim and owns the stopping decision. |

: **The card indexes records, it does not replace them:** each field points at something a reviewer can open, and a field the study never declared stays visibly empty rather than being filled in after the fact. {#tbl-design-loop-card-fields tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

The two weakest rows are the most useful lines in the table. A card that quietly drops a field it never declared, or that lets a claim and its evidence drift onto different metrics, makes a study look more governed than it was. Keeping the rows and recording what is missing is what turns the card from a summary into a review instrument, and it is why filling one honestly is uncomfortable.

A third weakness belongs to the instrument rather than to this study. None of the twelve fields is named for the mechanism account, so what Explain produces reaches a reviewer through three rows instead of one. Ablation runs belong under evidence, carrying the provenance any other run carries. An ablation that failed to reproduce the claimed mechanism belongs with the rejected alternatives. And what the mechanism licenses belongs under what the evidence supports, because a result nobody has explained supports a narrower conclusion than the same result with an ablation behind it. A card whose supporting row names a measured delta and no mechanism has recorded a correlation, and the failures above are what a correlation costs. Whether the card should carry a thirteenth field for this is unsettled. What it does today is index the mechanism account less directly than it indexes the evidence, which is something a reviewer has to know in order to look for it.

The card also has a machine-readable form, so a study can carry one without retyping it. A blank [template](https://arch2.mlsysbook.ai/design-loop-card/template.yaml) and its [Markdown counterpart](https://arch2.mlsysbook.ai/design-loop-card/template.md) hold the record in structured form, a [JSON schema](https://arch2.mlsysbook.ai/schemas/design-loop-card.v2.schema.json) describes it, and the [filled card](https://arch2.mlsysbook.ai/examples/design-loop-cards/array-study-v2.yaml) for the executed study in @sec-running-the-loop is the worked reference. Treat the twelve fields above as the contract and the schema as one way to write them down. The schema carries extra keys that automated checking needs, and it lets a card leave some of the twelve unfilled. A card can therefore pass validation without declaring all twelve, which is the gap the empty feedback-budget row records. Validation checks the shape of a card, not whether the study behind it declared enough.

![**A design-loop card indexes one architecture study.** It points readers to the study scope, claim, execution process, evidence, and decision owner.](images/F4b-design-loop-card-example){#fig-design-loop-card-example width="85%" fig-alt="A compact study index card for the Lighthouse prompt, listing twelve fields from intent through rejection checks and the accountable decision."}

A design-loop card cannot settle every dispute, but it can show a later reviewer which records a contested result actually disclosed. The card helps reviewers locate missing scope or evidence, preventing the name or capability of a model from becoming a substitute for adequate architectural evidence.

### Closing the Loop

The red return path in @fig-ontology-loop represents the most important element of the entire lifecycle: what happens when the architect looks at the design-loop card and *rejects* the AI's candidate. The lifecycle is not a static waterfall; it is a continuous learning loop.

When a candidate fails review, the negative evidence is fed directly back into the start. If the failure was due to an out-of-distribution proxy hallucination, the Explore stage uses the formatted negative evidence to update its Uncertainty Quantification and refit its surrogate. If the failure occurred because the original constraints were physically impossible, the human architect uses the rejected design-loop card to formulate a narrower, more realistic claim, and the cycle begins anew.

## Open Research Questions

The lifecycle in this chapter is a framework, and a framework earns trust by being tested. These questions are where its own machinery remains unproven.

**Theme 1: Replayable Studies and Transferable Rejections.** The design-loop card is one proposal for what a study must declare, and whether a stranger can re-run and challenge a study from it remains untested. A preserved rejection raises the same problem in reverse, since a negative trace earns its storage only if a later study can tell whether the rejection still holds.

- What is the smallest set of declarations that lets an independent architect replay an architecture study and reach the same rejection?
- How should a rejected candidate record the conditions under which its rejection still holds, so a later study can reuse it instead of paying for the same dead end?

**Theme 2: The Economics of Recording at Machine Volume.** The inner loop turns thousands of times, and the rule that no expensive run may be wasted implies recording every one of them. What that record costs and what it buys at machine volume, rather than at the pace of a hand-run study, has not been measured. The card's machine-readable form is weaker than the prose it serializes, since it marks almost nothing as required and would not catch a study that never declared an entry at all.

- At what volume of candidates does preserving every run and its provenance cost more than the search it saves?
- Which entries of a study record can a validator check mechanically, and which can only be attested by the architect who ran the study?

**Theme 3: Falsifiable Mechanism Accounts.** This chapter separates explanation from evaluation and requires an account a later run could contradict, but attribution methods such as SHAP explain the surrogate rather than the silicon. The account is also hostage to what the run kept, since telemetry discarded during evaluation prices the mechanism question at a second full run.

- Which ablations can an agent run on its own tools to show that a proposed mechanism, rather than an artifact of the simulator, produced a measured gain?
- Which intermediate telemetry must a run retain to keep a mechanism testable later, given that the retention decision is made before anyone knows which mechanism will need testing?

**Theme 4: Mechanical Checks on Judgment Calls.** Deciding that exploration has genuinely finished, or that the evidence justifies moving a candidate into implementation, is judgment today, and no recorded signal yet lets a check flag a premature transition. Claim scope is the same gap in another costume.

- Which recorded signals would let an automatic check flag a premature move from exploration into implementation?
- How can a claim's scope be encoded so that a tool detects when a result has been generalized beyond the workload and corner that produced it?

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="The loop cannot grant itself authority"}
A design loop may execute any stage it is given, but it cannot widen its own scope, waive its own checks, or authorize its own commitment. Every enlargement of what the loop may do is a decision made outside the loop, by a named owner, on recorded evidence.
:::

The Architecture 2.0 lifecycle gives an agent real initiative inside the loop while keeping the checks that verify its work, the claim it is tested against, and the final authority outside its reach. What holds the six stages apart is not the order they run in. Each fails to a different check and can fail while the other five pass, so a study that stops tells an architect which repair is needed rather than only that something went wrong. That test is also what a reader should carry to any other decomposition, this one included. Ask what can reject the work at each stage, and fold the stage that cannot answer. The same test explains the two speeds, because the three stages a machine can check unattended are exactly the three that turn thousands of times without a person in the room.

The stage this argument most has to defend is Explain, and it is the one a study under schedule pressure surrenders first. A number that cleared its check has not yet shown that the design produced it, and the runs that would settle it are additional runs, so the account has to be budgeted before the search starts rather than requested after it ends. The telemetry that makes it answerable has to be chosen even earlier, while the expensive run is still executing.

Two of the lifecycle's cheapest moves are also the easiest to skip. The analytic ceiling is the least expensive rejection check available, because a claim that cannot clear an envelope calculation ends the study before a single tool runs. And a rejected candidate carries the same provenance as a passing one, because what a study keeps, including the runs that failed, is what tells a later reader where the design space was actually searched. The twelve-field card then indexes the finished study, and the fields it never declared stay visibly empty, because those gaps are the study's real boundary.

What the lifecycle never does is convert rigor into permission. A study that escalates from an envelope estimate to a cycle-accurate run has raised its fidelity and not its authority, because what a result may commit to was fixed by the claim the study bounded at the outset rather than by the cost of the tool that later confirmed it. Passing cleanly through all six stages yields a defensible record of one bounded comparison. It does not yield a general finding, and an architect who reads a completed study as though it did has drawn a conclusion the lifecycle was built to prevent. Nor is the decomposition itself established. The argument for six seams rests on failure modes this chapter can name and cases it can point to, not on independent groups running the stages and reporting where the seams held.

The six stages describe one study's passage from formulation to defense, and the chapters that follow build the machinery those stages consume (@tbl-lifecycle-map). They decompose the work inside a bounded study rather than organize the book, which runs instead on what each chapter equips the loop with and on who holds authority over the result. Two chapters therefore appear nowhere in the table, because they act on the whole lifecycle rather than supply any one stage. @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales establishes why the loop needs assistance before any stage runs, and @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack resets every stage's settings as the next decision becomes slower to evaluate and harder to reverse.

| **Lifecycle stage** | **What the loop must supply** | **Where the book builds it** | **An RL reader's term** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Formulate | the bounded study and its claim | this chapter | the task |
| Explore | represented design state and search methods | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | state, policy |
| Implement | an execution environment over real tools | @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces | environment |
| Evaluate | feedback converted into evidence | @sec-feedback-verification-trust, @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect | reward, with a caveat |
| Explain | a tested mechanism account | @sec-running-the-loop | (none) |
| Defend | ownership and commitment | @sec-what-architect-owns | (none) |

: **One spine, six stages:** each stage names what the design loop must supply and the chapter that builds it; Explain is exercised inside the worked study rather than in a chapter of its own. The right column is a one-time translation for readers arriving from reinforcement learning; the book's own vocabulary is the lifecycle. {#tbl-lifecycle-map tbl-colwidths="[16,32,36,16]"}

A study cannot be explored until the design state is something a method can see and change. That state is what @sec-data-representations-world-models supplies, along with the knowledge sorted around it by authority, provenance, and freshness, so a method perceives the limits of its world rather than inferring them.
